Film and video editing jobs vary considerably: time-sensitive news and sports edits; narrative refinement for feature documentaries and series; extensive footage selection for variety and reality shows; multiple versions of advertising and brand films; batch production of online short videos and livestream excerpts; and standardized delivery of corporate promotional and instructional videos. They differ in genre and duration, material volume, simultaneous work with camera teams, additional color grading and mixing responsibilities, and project-based or office-based employment. Before comparing jobs, check the genre and delivery channels, material and project management methods, software and plugin environments, licensing and confidentiality constraints, schedules and overtime rhythm, and pay and credit agreements.

Test this through a paper exercise: given an entirely fictional editing work order specifying genre and running time, material count and total duration, director or client priorities, licensing and confidentiality restrictions, delivery formats and timecode requirements, and available software and hardware, write material review and annotation methods, a structure and pacing plan, sound-picture alignment and graphic treatment considerations, a technical checking and export checklist, versioning and backup methods, and decisions requiring director, producer, or legal confirmation.

Signals worth considering: willingness to review materials for long periods and repeatedly fine-tune them, proactively suggest structural plans within clear requirements, manage versions and backups properly, and accept repeated rework. Signals calling for caution: focusing only on personal aesthetic preferences, treating licensing and confidentiality as steps that can be bypassed, and resisting version management and delivery specifications.
This card is a career exploration reference. It does not constitute a hiring decision, ability rating, or conclusion on copyright or delivery compliance.

First consider whether you are willing to spend long periods making precise screen-based adjustments, accept project deadline work and repeated revisions, and use materials within licensing and delivery requirements. Test this with this page's paper exercise and seven-day tasks.

Film and video editors' daily work centers on four areas: materials, structure, sound, and delivery. First import footage and review and annotate it by scene, camera position, and content to establish usable scope; determine narrative sequence according to scripts, storyboards, or director intentions, choosing the best shots from each scene to build sequences; trim segments to running time and adjust cuts and pacing for natural continuity; align dialogue, music, and sound effects to pictures and manage their relationship; use editing, titling, switching, and effects systems for graphic treatment; check timecodes, key numbers, and delivery parameters before exporting masters; coordinate with camera, sound recording, music, and visual effects departments, attending screenings with directors and producers and completing repeated revisions; maintain project files, versions, and material backups; and deliver and archive under contracts.

Work context | Film and video editors work at editing stations in postproduction rooms, editing suites, or media organizations, cycling through material review and annotation, narrative structure, pacing and cuts, sound-picture alignment and graphic treatment, technical checks and export, collaboration, and revisions.
Workplaces | Film and postproduction companies, broadcasting and online audiovisual platforms, advertising and brand content teams, corporate video departments, and freelancers' own workstations.
Working conditions | Predominantly prolonged sitting and screen work (O*NET: 62% sit continually or almost continually, 34% more than half the time); schedules are mainly regular (97%); 62% of respondents work 40 hours per week and 38% more than 40 hours, with concentrated overtime around project and broadcast deadlines; precision and accuracy are highly important (51% extremely important, 42% very important); 71% face strict deadlines daily; 58% have constant contact with others, 13% most of the time, and 18% occasionally; 90% report that equipment speed is not at all important to work pace.
Main work objects | Filmed footage and recorded sound, scripts and storyboards, timecodes and key numbers, editing and effects project files, title and motion graphics templates, master delivery specifications, and backup media.
Collaboration | Directors and producers, camera and sound recording personnel, music and sound effects editors, visual effects and motion graphics staff, broadcast and platform contacts, and postproduction technical supervisors.
Tools and materials | Nonlinear editing and postproduction software (including compositing, color grading, and image processing tools), titling and master output tools, storage and backup equipment, delivery specifications, and source material lists.
Applicable requirements | Copyright and licensing requirements for footage and music, likeness and privacy use restrictions, confidentiality clauses agreed with clients or platforms, master delivery and broadcast technical specifications, content classification and review requirements, and employment, wage, and working time rules (including project-based daily pay and credit agreements).
Recordkeeping requirements | Material and license registers, project files and version records, revision and review records, export and delivery records, and backup and archive records must be retained under project or employer procedures.

entries.answer: Responsibilities differ: this occupation mainly handles material annotation, narrative editing, sound-picture alignment, and delivery in postproduction; film and video camera operators primarily frame and shoot on location; multimedia artists and animators primarily create and composite animation and visual assets; producers and directors organize projects and coordinate creative work; media programming directors manage medium- and long-term program scheduling and content; art directors oversee overall visual direction; audio and video equipment technicians install, configure, and maintain equipment; broadcast and sound technicians focus on broadcast and transmission technology; and sound engineering technicians focus on recording and audio technology.

entries.answer: A more precise assessment is that tools will take over processes such as material organization, transcription and subtitles, and retrieval, while the occupation mainly experiences augmentation and a shift toward higher-level responsibilities. The ILO's 2023 study shows task exposure varies considerably between occupations, and technical feasibility does not mean producers have adopted the technology. Structural tradeoffs, pacing judgments, screening communication, and licensing and confidentiality checks require experience and accountability. The conclusion is changing work methods and responsibility priorities rather than wholesale replacement.

entries.answer: No. The median is the midpoint of workers' wage distribution within the same statistical period, not a starting wage. Schedules are mainly regular, but overtime concentrates around project and broadcast deadlines. Some workers take project or freelance assignments; individual income depends on genre, project duration, and pay method (O*NET: 62% of respondents work 40 hours weekly, 38% more than 40 hours, and 71% face strict deadlines daily).
